Rapid and Facile Spectrophotometric
Method for the Selective Determination of
Peroxymonosulfate, Peroxydisulfate and
Hydrogen Peroxide in Ternary Mixtures
Anna M Dorfmüller
1

1

1

Abstract
Peroxides such as peroxydisulfate (PDS), peroxymonosulfate (PMS) and hydrogen peroxide
(H2O2) are important bulk oxidants used in wastewater treatment, bleaching or leaching. In
many of these processes and during electrosynthesis, they often coexist in complex mixtures.
Selective quantiﬁcation of each peroxide constitutes a fundamental step towards understanding
and optimizing these processes. However, achieving selectivity poses a major analytical
challenge since most quantiﬁcation methods rely on the oxidative properties towards indicators
and interference through coexisting peroxides is common. In this study, the diﬀerent iodide
oxidation kinetics of PDS, PMS, and H 2O2 were utilized to diﬀerentiate between them. Time-
resolved spectrophotometry at 350 nm under optimized assay conditions was established
as a prerequisite for achieving suﬃcient selectivity and reliable quantiﬁcation. Employing
low iodide concentrations and short reaction times, enable selective PMS quantiﬁcation. By
adding molybdate catalyst, the determination of H2O2 is realized. Finally, the PDS concentration
is derived from the total peroxide content obtained under optimized assay conditions by
subtracting the H2O2 and PMS concentration. The assay sensitivities reach 7.62 × 103 M−1 (PMS),
7.68 × 103 M−1 (H2O2) and 4.1 × 103 M−1 (PDS) while the limit of quantiﬁcation is as low as 6.6 µM
(PMS), 3.9 µM (H2O2) and 17 µM (PDS). The degree of interference caused by coexisting peroxides
was thorougly investigated and the proposed quantiﬁcation procedure was successfully applied
to real electrolysis samples. The simplicity and reliability of the developed method enables high-
throughput screening of electrodes, electrolytes or reaction conditions and allows quality control
of processes.

Rapid and Facile Spectrophotometric Method for the 
Selective Determination of  Peroxymonosulfate, Peroxy-
disulfate and Hydrogen Peroxide in Ternary Mixtures 
 
Anna M. Dorfmüllera, Mark M. Pradjaa, Christian Modrzynskia, Jonathan Z. Bloha,* 
 
a DECHEMA- Forschungsinstitut, Benzstraße 1-3, 61352 Bad Homburg v. d. Höhe, Germany 
* Corresponding Author, Email: jonathan.bloh@dechema.de 
 
 
ABSTRACT: Peroxides such as peroxydisulfate (PDS), peroxymonosulfate (PMS) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) are important bulk 
oxidants used in wastewater treatment, bleaching or leaching. In many of these processes and during electrosynthesis, they often coexist 
in complex mixtures. Selective quantification of each pero xide constitutes a fundamental step towards understanding and optimizing 
these processes. However, achieving selectivity poses a major  analytical challenge since most quantification methods rely on the 
oxidative properties towards indicators and interference through coexisting peroxides is common. In this study, the different iodide 
oxidation kinetics of PDS, PMS, and H2O2 were utilized to differentiate between  them. Time-resolved spectrophotometry at 350 nm 
under optimized assay conditions w as established as a prerequisite for achieving sufficient selectivity and reliable quantification.  
Employing low iodide concentrations and short reaction times, enable selective PMS quantification. By adding molybdate catalyst, the 
determination of H2O2 is realized. Finally, the PDS concentration is derived from the total peroxide content obtained under optimized 
assay conditions by subtracting the H2O2 and PMS concentration. The assay sensitivities reach 7.62 × 103 M−1 (PMS), 7.68 × 103 M−1 
(H2O2) and 4.1 × 103 M−1 (PDS) while the limit of quantification is as low as 6.6 µM (PMS), 3.9 µM (H2O2) and 17 µM (PDS). The 
degree of interference caused by coexisting peroxides was th orougly investigated and the proposed quantification procedure was 
successfully applied to real electrolysis samples.  The simplicity and reliability of the developed method enable s high-throughput 
screening of electrodes, electrolytes or reaction conditions and allows quality control of processes.

1 Introduction 
Peroxydisulfate (PDS , S2O82−), perox ymonosulfate (PMS, 
HSO5−) and hydrogen peroxide  (H2O2) are strong oxidants that 
are commonly used for bleaching[1, 2] , polymerization [3, 4] , 
etching[5, 6], leaching[7, 8] or wastewater treatment[9, 10]. Recently, 
especially advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) for wastewater 
treatment using persulfates  (PDS and PMS)  have gained 
increasing interest. [11, 12]  Thereby, complex mixture s are 
commonly used , which  can contain PDS, PMS and hydrogen 
peroxide simultaneously because binary mixtures (of PDS and 
H2O2 as well PMS and H 2O2) have been demonstrated to be  
beneficial in sulfate-radical based AOPs.[10, 13, 14]  
Another reason for the coexistence of several peroxides in 
complex mixtures is given through the fast hydrolysis  (Eq. (1)) 
of PDS to fo rm PMS  in acidic conditions. PMS further 
hydrolyses forming hydrogen peroxide through Eq. (2), which is 
reversible and may lead to the in situ formation of PMS in sulfate 
containing peroxide solutions. As such, complex mixtures of 
these peroxides may arise even if only one reagent is used 
initially. Likewise, in electrosynthesis, the simultaneous 
generation of various peroxides is observed in acidic conditions 
[15–17] and interconversion through Eq. (1) and (2) commonly 
occurs during electrolysis. [18–20] 
 S2O82− + H+ + H2O → HSO5− + H2SO4 (1) 
 HSO5− + H+ + H2O ⇌ H2O2 + H2SO4 (2) 
These complex mixtures of PDS, PMS and H 2O2 can be 
challenging to quantify due to mutual interference s because 
most quantification methods rely on the oxidative nature of these 
species towards indicators such as iodide  or permanganate.  
Meanwhile, their chemical similarity such as the shared O -O 
peroxide bond, makes it challenging to distinguish between 
them with many analysis methods such as infrared spectroscopy. 
Therefore, m ost quantifi cation methods target only the total 
peroxide concentration or study singular solutions of one 
peroxide and potential interference in mixtures with other 
peroxides is not considered. But selective quantification is  
important for u nderstanding reaction mechanism s and kinetics 
as well as for  optimizing process conditions . Commonly used 
detection methods include titration, UV/VIS spectroscopy, 
polarography or ion chromatography.[21, 22]  
Concerning titration , several titrants have been reported t o 
facilitate selective quantif ication of  H2O2 in presence of PDS 
such as ceric sulfate [23, 24]  or potassium permanganate [24]. 
Nevertheless, application to ternary mixtures can be problematic 
as the interference of PMS is unclear. More specific is the multi-
step titration developed by Wang et al. [25] for the simultaneous 
determination of PDS, PMS and H2O2 in mixtures, which is 
based on iodometry. Nonetheless, titration often requires big 
sample volumes and is tedious to perform. This method also 
consumes the species in question, which may lead to the 
formation of additional PMS or H 2O2 through the equilibrium 
(2) during titration, particularly since the method takes 
significant time. Furthermore, high relative errors arising fr om 
rapid titration, pH or temperature variations , as well as narrow 
quantification range s and high detection  limits, often make it 
unsuitable for low -concentrated samples , e.g. in 
electrosynthesis.[22] 
Other detection methods such as polarography [26, 27]  or ion 
chromatography[28, 29] have been proposed for the quantification 
of PDS but require expensive instrumentation and potential 
interference of H2O2 or PMS is often not studied.  For example, 
H2O2 is expected to interfere with polarographic method s, 
making it unsuitable for analysing peroxide mixtures.[22] In 
addition, commonly used electrolytes for persulfate 
electrosynthesis, such as H 2SO4 and ammonium salts , cause 
interference and therefore polarograph y cannot be used for 
electrolysis samples.[27] 
Faster and more reliable quantification of ternary peroxide 
mixtures can be realized with UV/VIS spectroscopy. Multiple 
colorimetric reagents such as  N,N-diethyl-p-phenylenediamine 
(DPD)[22], 2,2 '-azino-bis(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonate) 
(ABTS)[30], rhodamine B [31], iodide[32] or titan yl salts[33] have 
been established  for the quantification of peroxides. Some 
reagents are known to selectively react only with one peroxide, 
e. g. titan yl salts with H 2O2. However, with the highly acidic 
measurement conditions used, the hydrolysis of PMS to H 2O2 
(Eq. (2)) is accelerated which can falsify the H2O2 concentration 
if the reaction time is too long. Other colorimetric reagents, such 
as iodide , are non -selective and  the standard methods often 
estimate only the total peroxide concentration. 
Nevertheless, w e propose a new spectrophotometric method 
using iodide as the only indicator to selectively measure PDS, 
PMS and H 2O2 in ternary mixtures.  Iodide is a widely used 
reagent to quantify oxidative species photometrically or via 
titration. It is well known that all three peroxides (PDS, PMS 
and H 2O2) react with iodide to stoichiometrically form yellow 
triiodide (Eq.  (3) – (6)) with a maximum absorbance at 
350 nm.[21–23]  
 HSO5− + 2I− + H+ →  SO42− + I2 + H2O (3) 
 H2O2 + 2I− + 2 H+ → I2 + 2H2O (4) 
 S2O82− + 2I− → 2SO42− + I2 (5) 
 I2 + I− ⇌ I3− (6) 
Several spectrophotometric methods using iodide as indicator 
have already been described that can measure PMS, H2O2[34] and 
PDS[32, 35, 36] in solutions containing only one peroxide. Recently 
Chen et al. [21] discussed the selectivity of the photometric 
quantification with iodide for binary mixtures of PDS, PMS and 
H2O2. They found that with optimized KI concentrations , PMS 
could be selectively determined in presence of H2O2 or PDS, due 
to the much slower reaction of the latter compounds.  
Here we present a new ly developed method with optimized 
reaction conditions, which enables selective determination of 
PDS, PMS and H2O2 in ternary mixtures. Inspired by the 
selective determination of peracetic acid and H 2O2 with iodide 
by Xiao et al.[37], this is achieved through kinetic differentiation, 
as the reaction rate of iodide oxidation differs significantly 
between the three peroxides. Furthermore, the difference in rate 
of reaction can be optimized through the addition of specific 
catalysts such as molybdate or bicarbonate . The degree of 
interference caused by the presence of the other peroxides was 
thoroughly investigated for the quantification of PDS, PMS and 
H2O2 with the proposed assays . The application of the 
quantification method  was verified with  real samples arising 
from electrolysis and the subsequent hydrolysis of the 
electrogenerated persulfates to H2O2 could be followed precisely 
with the proposed method.

2 Materials and Methods 
Chemicals 
Commercial hydrogen peroxide solution (30  wt%) purchased 
from Carl Roth GmbH was used as calibration standard as well 
as p eroxymonosulfate in the form of Oxone® -salt purchased 
from Thermo Fisher Scientific and ammonium peroxydisulfate 
((NH4)2S2O8) purchased from VWR Avantor. The H2O2 
concentration was standardized with iodometric titration  
described in detail in the SI. The concentrations of the PDS and 
PMS stock solutions were determined with iodometric titration 
as well , following the method of Thompson [38]. For the 
spectrophotometric assays, potassium iodide (KI) and potassium 
bicarbonate (KHCO3) were obtained from Alfa Aesar. 
Ammonium molybdate tetrahydrate ((NH4)6Mo7O24∙4H2O) was 
purchased from Acros Organics. Potassium dihydrogen 
phosphate, anhydrous (KH 2PO4) was obtained from VWR 
Avantor. Diluted sulfuric acid (H2SO4) from Carl Roth was used 
as electrolyte for the electrochemical experiments. All reagents 
were of analytical grade and were used without further 
purification. Ultrapure water (18 MΩ cm) was produced from a 
PURELAB ultra water purification system (ELGA LabWater).  
Apparatus 
All UV/VIS measurements were performed on a microplate 
reader from Agilent (PowerWave  HT, formerly BioTek) using 
96 well -plates (polystyrene). The electrochemical experiment 
was carried out in an H-cell setup with a 20 cm² BDD-anode (2 
× 10 cm² front and back,  expanded metal) from W&L coating 
systems GmbH and a carbon felt cathode as counter electrode. A 
Hg/Hg2SO4-electrode serve d as reference electrode in the 3-
electrode setup. The distance between working and counter 
electrode was approximately 10  cm and the half -cells were 
separated through a cation exchange membrane from Fumatech 
BWT (F-930rfd). The anolyte and catholyte were both 100  mL 
of 5 M H2SO4. An Ivium-n-Stat potentiostat was used to apply a 
constant current of 2 A. 
Experimental Procedure 
Preparation of Stock Solutions 
A 1.2 M KI stock solution was prepared by dissolving 19.9 g of 
potassium iodide in 100  mL of ultrapure water. The 0.1  M 
phosphate buffer stock solution with pH 4.0 was obtained by 
dissolving 68 g of KH2PO4 in 1 L of ultrapure water. 0.124 g of 
(NH4)6Mo7O24∙4H2O was dissolved in 20 mL of ultrapure water 
to obtain a 35 mM molybdate stock solution. The indicator stock 
mix for the KI -assay (mix 1, see Table  S1), which  is used to  
determine PMS, was prepared by mixing 14  mL phosphate 
buffer stock (0.5  M, pH 4.0) with 1  mL KI stock (1.2  M). The 
KI concentration in the obtained mix 1 is 80 mM. The indicator 
stock for the KI/Mo-assay (mix 2), which determines the PMS 
and H 2O2 concentration, was prepared by mixing 13.83  mL 
phosphate buffer stock (0.5  M, pH 4.0) with 667  µL KI stock 
(1.2 M) and 500  µL molybdate stock  (35 mM). Mix 2, as 
obtained, has a KI concentration of 53  mM and a molybdate 
concentration of 1.2 mM. Lastly, mix 3 for the KI/KHCO3-assay 
was prepared by mixing 12.5  mL KI stock (1.2  M) and 7.5 mL 
KHCO3 (2 M). The obtained mix 3 contains KI and KHCO 3 at 
concentrations of 0.75 M.  
Under dark conditions, the stock solutions remain stable and can 
be stored in the refrigerator for several weeks.  Note that the 
autooxidation of iodide cannot be completely inhibited, 
therefore the solutions should be freshly prepared on a regular 
basis. In this work the indicator stocks were discarded and 
reprepared when the absorbance of the blank at 350  nm was 
above 0.15. 
PMS Determination (KI-assay) 
100 µL of a sample containing various peroxides were placed in 
a well in a 96 well-plate. To reduce uncertainties, replicate 
determination was done by preparing at least two wells with the 
same sample. In addition, the background must also be measured 
in situ to enable baseline correction. For this purpose, 100 µL of 
the matrix ( water or the respective electrolyte) were added to 
another well. Subsequently, 150 µL of mix 1 w ere added to all 
prepared wells and the absorbance at 350  nm (25  °C) was 
measured immediately afterwards. Note that it is important to 
measure the absorbance as fast as possible after the addition of 
indicator to selectively measure PMS concentrations. After 
baseline correcting the measured absorbance, the PMS 
concentration can be calculated using the calibration curve  in 
Fig. 2 a). Note that calibration is specific to the employed sample 
container due to the employed path length and should be verified 
for each employed setup.  
H2O2 Determination (KI/Mo-assay) 
To determine the H2O2 concentration in mixtures  containing 
PMS as well , the above-mentioned KI-assay must first be 
performed to measure the PMS concentration. Subsequently, the 
KI/Mo-assay measuring the combined concentration of  PMS 
and H2O2 is proposed as follows. 100 µL of the peroxide sample 
were added to a well in the 96  well-plate. As with the PMS 
measurement described above, replicate determination should 
be done, and the background must be measured in situ. 150 µL 
of mix 2 were added to all the prepared wells. The absorbance at 
350 nm was measured directly after the addition of indicator mix 
2 for 3 minutes in 10 s intervals at 25 °C. The mean absorbance 
between 2 and 3  minutes was baseline corrected and used to 
calculate the total concentration of  PMS and H 2O2 via the 
calibration curve of the KI/Mo -assay (see Fig. 2 b). Based on 
Eq. (7), the H 2O2 concentration can be derived from the 
difference between the combined  concentration of PMS and 
H2O2 measured with the KI/Mo -assay and the  PMS 
concentration measured with the KI-assay. 
 [H2O2] = [PMS + H2O2]KI/Mo − [PMS]KI (7) 
PDS Determination (KI/KHCO3-assay) 
50 µL of sample were mixed with 200 µL of mix 3 in a 96 well-
plate. Replicate determination is recommended and the  
respective background should be  measured in situ  by mixing 
50 µL of water or respective electrolyte with 200  µL of mix 3. 
The absorbance at 350 nm (25 °C) was measured for 8 minutes 
in 10  s intervals immediately after the addition of indicator. 
After baseline correcting the data, the mean absorbance between 
5 and 8  minutes was used to calculate the total peroxide 
concentration using the calibration curve in Fig. 2 c). Lastly, the 
PDS concentration can be determined via Eq. (8) by subtracting 
the combined concentration of PMS and H2O2 measured with 
the KI/Mo-assay from the total peroxide concentration measured 
with the KI/KHCO3-assay. 
[PDS] = [PMS + H2O2 + PDS]KI/KHCO3 
− [PMS + H2O2]KI/Mo (8)

3 Results and Discussion 
Selective Determination through Kinetic 
Measurements  
The reaction rate of iodide oxidation differs between PDS, PMS 
and H 2O2, which can be used to selectively quantify each 
peroxide separately. It is known that the kinetics of iodide 
oxidation by PMS are significantly faster than the oxidation by 
PDS or H 2O2.[18, 39] Specifically, t he rate of reaction between 
H2O2 and iodide (9.5 × 10–3 M–1 s–1)[34] is reported to be 6 orders 
of magnitude slower than  the reaction rate of PMS and iodide 
(1.01 × 103 M–1 s–1)[40]. In the past, the fast oxidation behaviour 
of PMS has been used to distinguish between PMS and PDS [38] 
as well as between PMS and H2O2[39] via iodometric titration but 
ternary mixtures were not investigated.  
Herein, the new ly developed spectroscopic method enables  
spectrophotometric differentiation between all three peroxides. 
The differentiation is achieved by selecting three different 
reaction conditions and catalysts which enable selective 
determination of either PMS alone, PMS and H 2O2, or the total 
peroxide concentration. These th ree measurement procedures  
(KI-assay, KI/Mo-assay and KI/KHCO3-assay) were developed 
for ternary mixtures of PMS, PDS and H2O2 and are described 
in detail in the following. 
In Fig. 1 the absorbance at 350 nm is depicted for the three 
proposed assays resulting from the oxidation of iodide using 
equimolar amounts of PMS, PDS or H2O2. The absorbance is 
recorded with time resolution for the  reaction period after the 
addition of indicator mix to the samples.  
As can be seen in Fig. 1 a), even with  relatively low KI 
concentrations (80 mM), PMS shows quantitative conversion 
already after  short reaction time s (0 – 10 s). This enables  a 
selective determination of PMS in presence of both, H2O2 and 
PDS, due to their much slower reaction rates . Fig. 1 a) 
demonstrates that after 10 s of reaction time, equimolar amounts 
of H 2O2 or PDS result in insignificantly small absorbances at 
350 nm which is negligible for the PMS determination. Further 
studies of the interference caused by higher concentrations of 
H2O2 or PDS in mixtures with PMS are discussed in the chapter 
on Degree of Interference.  
For a selective quantification of H 2O2 in presence of PDS, 
kinetic differentiation of iodide -oxidation must be found.  By 
adding molybdate (1.2  mM) as a catalyst to the KI -assay, the 
H2O2 oxidation is significantly accelerated, as previously 
observed by Copper et al.[34], while the iodide oxidation by PDS 
is not influenced (see Fig. 1 b). It appears that the molybdenum 
peroxy complex selectively forms form reacting with H2O2 (and 
possibly PMS) only, but not PDS. The reason may lie in the fact 
that PDS does not feature a terminal peroxide, which could form 
a peroxide anion and thus has a much lower nucleophilicity. This 
enables the determination of  the combined concentration of 
H2O2 and PMS after a reaction time of 120 – 180 seconds. The 
chosen reaction time results from two different effects. On the 
one hand the reaction time needs to be sufficient to detect all 
H2O2 present, hence the plateau of absorbance must be reached, 
which is the case after approximately 150  s. On the other hand, 
the reaction time should be as short as possible to reduce 
inaccuracy caused by PDS slowly oxidizing iodide (see Fig. 
1 b).  
Lastly, a method was developed to measure the total peroxide 
concentration independent of the mixture composition. Thereby, 
the iodide oxidation  rate by PDS must be increased to allow 
measurements in less than 15 minutes as too long reaction times 
lead to the decomposition of triiodide. We found that bicarbonate 
is a very effective, non -selective catalyst for promoting iodide 
oxidation, making it suitable for this purpose. T he reaction rate 
of iodide oxidation by PDS is also strongly dependent on the KI 
concentration[35], thus a fast determination of the total peroxide 
amount can be achieved when using KI concentrations as high 
as 0.75 M (see the chapter on Condition Optimization). In Fig. 1 
c) equal concentrations of PDS, PMS and H 2O2 in singular 
solutions result in the same maximum absorbance after 
300 – 480 seconds. The addition of KHCO3 catalyst is essential 
to achieve a reliable total peroxide determination and will be 
discussed in the following chapter on Condition Optimization. 
The absorbance spectra obtained for PMS measured with the KI-
assay, for H2O2 measured with the KI/Mo -assay and for PDS 
measured with the KI/KHCO 3-assay are depicted in the 
supporting information (Fig. S1).

Calibration 
Based on a PMS standard solution , calibration was performed 
using the KI -assay (see Fig. 2 a). The baseline-corrected 
absorbance at 350 nm resulting from PDS/H2O2 samples is also 
shown in Fig. 2 a) to demonstrate the selectivity of the assay.  A 
excellent linear correlation (R² = 0.9999) between the baseline-
corrected absorbance and the PMS concentration is detected for 
concentrations of up to 250 µM. The limit of detection (LOD) as 
well as the limit of quantification (LOQ) is calculated with Eq. 
(9) and Eq. (10) following IUPAC recommendations and 
ISO 11843–1.[41, 42] For the determination of PMS with the KI -
assay the LOD is 2.0 µM and the LOQ is accounted to be as low 
as 6.6 µM. This results in a quantification range of 7  – 250 µM 
for PMS with a high sensitivity (7.62 × 103 M−1).

σ is the standard deviation of the mean absorbance of ten blank 
samples measured with the respective assay and k is the slope of 
the respective calibration curve (Table S2). 
The calibration for the KI/Mo -assay was done using two 
separate standard solutions, one containing PMS and the other 
one containing H2O2 (see Fig. 2 b). Since the KI/Mo -assay 
allows for the simultaneous determination of PMS and H 2O2, 
both peroxides in singular solutions produce the same 
absorbance response  under the chosen assay conditions. 
Therefore, this procedure is effectively equivalent to replicate 
determinations of a single calibration curve . In the range of 
4 µM up to 250 µM the joint calibration curve was linear for the 
detection of PMS and H2O2, again with an excellent coefficient 
of determination (R 2) of 0.9993. The  quantification is highly 
sensitive (7.68 × 103 M−1) with a LOD of 1.2 µM and a LOQ of 
3.9 µM.  
Three standard solutions containing either  only PMS, H2O2 or 
PDS were used for the calibration of the KI/KHCO 3-assay (see 
Fig. 2 c). Similar to  the KI/Mo -assay, this is equivalent to 
replicate calibration, since the KI/KHCO 3-assay determines the 
total peroxide concentration independent of the peroxide 
species. The equivalence of the different peroxides in the 
detection is again highlighted by the outstanding  linear 
correlation (R²  = 0.9999) between the absorbance at 350  nm 
(baseline-corrected) and the respective peroxide concentration. 
The concentration range  in this case is  17 µM – 500 µM, the  
calculated LOD is 5.1 µM and the LOQ amounts to 17 µM with 
a high sensitivity of 4.1 × 103 M−1.  
Condition Optimization 
In general, the pH value is of importance for iodide assays  and 
must be kept in an optimal range. On the one hand the pH value 
should not be too low because autoxidation of I− by air (Eq. (11)) 
becomes a noticeable issue at low pH, potentially distorting the 
measurements. 
 4I− + O2 + 4H+ → 2I2 + 2H2O (11) 
On the other hand, at pH values greater than 8, triiodide is 
increasingly decomposed by the  disproportionation reaction 
shown in Eq. (12).[36] 
 3I3− + 6OH− → IO3− + 8I− + 3H2O (12) 
This underlines the significance of keeping an optimal pH range 
which is achieved in the proposed assays (KI- and KI/Mo-assay) 
through the addition of phosphate buffer with pH  4.0. The 
KI/KHCO3-assay is an exception as no phosphate buffer is used, 
due to kinetic reasons as well as the importance of diminishing 
autooxidation which will be discussed in detail in the following. 
Besides that, the two most important factors that need to be 
optimized to make selective peroxide determination possible are 
the reaction time and the KI concentration. For the total peroxide 
quantification with the KI/KHCO 3-assay, the KHCO 3 
concentration also has a significant influence (see Fig. 5) and 
optimal conditions were investigated. The effect of the KI 
concentration on the PDS, PMS and H2O2 determination as well 
as the KHCO3 concentration on the total peroxide determination 
are discussed in the following.

KI/KHCO3-Assay 
To accurately determine the total peroxide concentration of 
complex mixtures with different composition, equimolar 
concentrations of PDS, PMS or H2O2 should yield the same 
absorbance after reacting with iodide for a defined time interval. 
As the reaction rate between iodide and PDS is relatively slow 
for the conditions in both assays above, higher KI concentrations 
were evaluated which should enhance th e rate of reaction by 
PDS. Different KI concentrations ranging from 0.45  M to 
1.05 M were tested with resp ect to the mean absorbance after 
300 – 480 s caused by 250 µM PMS, 250 µM H2O2 or 250 µM 
PDS standard solutions (see Fig. 5 a).  
With increasing KI concentration, the iodide oxidation by PDS 
is accelerated as can be seen in Fig . S3 . When the KI 
concentration is below 0.75  M, the reaction rate of PDS and 
iodide is still too slow to reach a plateau after 8  minutes. 
Therefore, the mean absorbance after 300 – 480 s in Fig. 5 a) is 
lower for PDS than for PMS or H2O2. This makes accurate total 
peroxide determination impossible. Nevertheless, the KI 
concentration also shouldn’t be too high to diminish 
autooxidation of iodide by air.  Autooxidation becomes 
increasingly appreciable with high  KI concentrations which 
could decrease precision. Therefore, a concentration of 0.75  M 
KI was selected as optimal reaction condition for the total 
peroxide quantification with the proposed assay.  
By addition of KHCO 3, the autooxidation of iodide can be 
suppressed. This is particularly relevant when measuring 
samples from electrolysis, as usually strongly acidic electrolytes 
are used , which accelerate the autooxidation (see Eq . (11)).  
Fig. S4 shows the absorbance of a blank sample (50 µL H2O) for

the time frame of the proposed assay with KHCO 3 (pH 8) in 
comparison to when phosphate buffer (pH  4) is used. It depicts 
the relevance of pH control to dimmish autooxidation for precise 
measurements.

(13), t he influence of other peroxides (not intended to be 
measured) present in mixtures on the measured absorbance is

Exponential Modelling 
The high degree of interference of the KI/Mo -assay in the 
presence of PDS was caused by the overlapping kinetics of its 
reaction with iodide which become relevant when a large excess 
of PDS is present. However, by fitting the recorded absorbance 
curves with an exponential plot combined with a linear term, the 
degree of interference by PDS  can be minimized for the H 2O2 
quantification with the KI/Mo-assay. The curves are fitted with 
the following Eq. (14): 
  A(t) = A0 ∙ (1 − e−k ∙ (t + t0)) + m ∙ t (14) 
where A(t) resembles the absorbance curve with A0 being only 
the absorbance correlated to the iodide oxidation by H2O2 with 
the rate constant k and a time correction term t0 that considers 
the time between indicator mix addition and the first absorbance 
measurement (usually ⁓ 5 s). The separate linear term with the 
slope m simulates the slow iodide oxidation by PDS.  
Fig. 7 a) shows the fitted absorbance curves of a 125 µM H2O2 
sample with no PDS as well as in mixture with 500  µM and 
1 mM PDS. It depicts that the measured absorbance data is well 
described by Eq. (14) as well as the relevance of this modelling 
step as the mean absorbance after 120 – 180 s is significantly 
higher in presence of 1 mM PDS. This fit allows to separate the 
contributions of H2O2 and PDS to the total absorbances and thus 
enables selective H 2O2 quantification even in highly 
concentrated PDS samples.  This is demonstrated in Fig. 7 b), 
where the degree of interference is always below 5% for up to a 
20-fold excess of PDS. In this case the A0 parameter from the fit 
is used in place of the measured absorbance to exclude the PDS 
contribution. 
Besides a selective H 2O2 quantification, the exponential 
modelling also enables PDS determination with the KI/Mo -
assay. This would be less work intensive and a faster detection 
method because H2O2 and PDS can be detected simultaneously 
by one assay. PDS determination is possible by using the slope 
m of the linear term which is  only correlated to iodide being 
oxidized by PDS. This slope  shows a linear correlation (R² =  
0.9979) with the PDS concentration as depicted in Fig S8. The 
concentration of H2O2 does not affect the slope m obtained from 
the fitting  (Fig. S9). But there are some limitations as this 
method is only applicable if the PDS concentration is larger or 
in the same order  of magnitude as H2O2. When PDS is orders 
lower than H2O2, the quantification becomes inaccurate which 
can be seen in Fig. S10 by the large error bars of the calibration 
curve where samples with H2O2 excess where used. Traces of 
PDS cannot be reliably quantified using this modelling, so in this 
case it is better to perform the third assay (KI/KHCO 3) as well, 
to measure the PDS concentration separately.

Application to Real Samples 
Understanding the peroxide synthesis through electrolysis and 
investigating the kinetics of the PDS, PMS and H 2O2 
interconversions during electro-generation is of importance and 
can be realized with the proposed detection procedure. 
Furthermore, the hydrolysis of PDS to PMS and subsequently 
H2O2 (Eq. (1) & (2)) following electro -synthesis has recently 
gained interest to enable the production of optimal peroxide 
mixtures for instance  for leaching cathode material from 
lithium-ion batteries.[7]

To test the applicability of the proposed assays, 1 h electrolysis 
of 5 M H2SO4 was performed at 2 A (Fig. S11) in an H-cell setup 
with a 20 cm2 (2 × 10 cm2 front and back, expanded metal) BDD 
anode. Subsequently, the peroxide mixture was heated to 65 °C 
to promote the conversion reactions and the concentration 
changes through hydrolysis were detected. The PDS, PMS and 
H2O2 concentrations were measured using the KI‑, KI/Mo- and 
the KI/KHCO 3-assay, respectively, by triplicate determination. 
For validation purposes, the TiOSO4-assay was carried out  as 
well (Fig. S12). After sampling, the samples were immediately 
cooled in an ice bath to stop hydrolysis and then diluted with 
water to adjust the concentrations to the calibration range. 
After 1 h of electrolysis the total peroxide concentration reached 
229 ± 4. 6 mM with a current efficiency of 61% (for the 
calculation, see supplementary note 4). The product composition 
consisted of 159 ± 5.4 mM PDS, 69 ± 0.8 mM PMS and 0.77 ± 
0.02 mM H2O2 (see Fig. 8). Afterwards the peroxide mixture 
was heated to 65 °C for 1.5 h and samples were taken to measure 
every 10 minutes for the first hour. A last sample was taken after 
90 minutes.

4 Conclusion 
A simple, reliable and fast quantification method was 
established, achieving selective and precise  determination of 
PDS, PMS and H2O2 in ternary mixtures.  It was demonstrated 
that KI, as the only indicator, allows to spectrophotometrically 
quantify all three coexisting peroxides by kinetic differentiation 
with different catalysts at 350 nm. The measurement conditions 
have been optimized to improve the selectivity of each assay. 
PMS can be detected with a high sensitivity of 7.62 × 103 M−1 
and a limit of quantification  of 6.6 µM using the proposed KI -
assay. The highly sensitive quantification  (7.68 × 103 M−1) of 
H2O2 with the KI/Mo-assay is possible for concentrations higher 
3.9 µM. Based on the KI/ KHCO3-assay, PDS can be measured 
with a LOQ of 17 µM and a high sensitivity (4.1 × 103 M−1). The 
degree of interference  caused by  the coexistence of the other 
peroxides in up to 20-fold excess is minor or non-detectable for 
the KI- and the KI/KHCO3-assay as well as for the KI/Mo-assay 
with exponential modelling.  A successful application  of the 
proposed assays to samples arising from electrolysis was 
demonstrated and the results were validated with the TiOSO 4-
assay. 
The short reaction times of 0 – 10 seconds for the KI-assay, 2 – 
3 minutes for the KI/Mo-assay and 5 – 8 minutes for KI/KHCO3-
assay enable rapid quantification. Additionally, the use of  
microplate photometers allows the simultaneous quantification 
of multiple samples, making the proposed method very time and 
labour efficient and enabling high -throughput screening. The 
use of inexpensive, common and non-toxic reagents paired with 
low required sample volumes  and fast implementation make it 
an attractive tool for routine measurements of  samples with 
various PDS, PMS and H 2O2 compositions. Based on the 
developed quantification method the formation and conversion 
kinetics of these peroxides can easily be investigated for various 
reaction conditions and kinetic simulations of the peroxide 
electrosynthesis become possible.
